title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
author: Daniel Kahneman
summary: Exploration of two modes of thought: intuitive fast System 1 and deliberative slow System 2.

cards.front: Two Systems of Thought: Intuitive Fast vs. Deliberative Slow
cards.back: System 1 is fast, automatic, emotional, and involuntary. System 2 is slow, deliberate, effortful, and logical.
cards.takeaway: Cognitive bias thrives when we let intuitive System 1 make complex decisions requiring System 2 auditing.

cards.front: Cognitive Ease: Why Familiar Claims Feel Inherently True
cards.back: Cognitive Ease occurs when information feels familiar, clear, and effortless. It makes our brains lower critical defenses and accept claims without scrutiny.
cards.takeaway: Repeated falsehoods feel familiar, creating the illusion of objective truth.

cards.front: WYSIATI Principle: What You See Is All There Is
cards.back: 'What You See Is All There Is' — System 1 constructs coherent stories from whatever fragments are immediately available, disregarding unknown evidence.
cards.takeaway: Never make pivotal strategic choices without actively asking: 'What critical information is completely invisible here?'

cards.front: The Anchoring Effect: The Invisible Gravity of Initial Numbers
cards.back: Initial numbers introduced into consideration establish psychological gravity, disproportionately anchoring all subsequent estimates and compromises.
cards.takeaway: In negotiations or valuation, set the initial anchor first, or immediately debunk an aggressive opposing anchor before proceeding.

title: Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion
author: Robert Cialdini
summary: The six universal principles of ethical and unethical persuasion and behavioral compliance.

cards.front: The Reciprocity Rule: The Compelling Urge to Repay Debts
cards.back: Human cultures hold a deeply ingrained debt reflex: receiving an uninvited gift creates intense psychological discomfort until repaid with concessions.
cards.takeaway: Give genuine value first before asking for commitments, or spot when a free favor is actually a compliance trap.

cards.front: Social Proof: Looking to the Collective Under Uncertainty
cards.back: When people are uncertain, they look to the actions of similar peers to determine correct behavior, assuming the collective knows best.
cards.takeaway: Pluralistic ignorance emerges when a crowd witnesses an emergency and everyone stays passive because no one else is reacting.

cards.front: Commitment & Consistency: Small Stances Snowballing into Action
cards.back: Once a person takes even a trivial public stand or small action, immense internal pressure forces them to align future decisions with that initial stance.
cards.takeaway: The 'foot-in-the-door' technique works by winning microscopic approvals before demanding large commitments.

title: Atomic Habits
author: James Clear
summary: An easy and proven way to build good habits and break bad ones via compound micro-improvements.

cards.front: Systems Beat Goals: You Fall to the Level of Your Systems
cards.back: Goals are about the results you want to achieve. Systems are about the processes that lead to those results. Winners and losers have the same goals.
cards.takeaway: You do not rise to the level of your goals; you fall to the level of your systems.

cards.front: The 4 Laws of Behavior Change: Cue, Craving, Response, Reward
cards.back: Make it Obvious (Cue), Make it Attractive (Craving), Make it Easy (Response), Make it Satisfying (Reward).
cards.takeaway: To break a bad habit, invert the 4 laws: Make it invisible, unattractive, difficult, and unsatisfying.

cards.front: Identity-Based Habits: Changing Who You Are, Not Just What You Do
cards.back: True behavior change is identity change. You might start a habit because of motivation, but you'll only stick with it if it becomes part of who you are.
cards.takeaway: Every action you take is a vote for the type of person you wish to become.

title: Economics in One Lesson
author: Henry Hazlitt
summary: Economic analysis distilled to tracing secondary and tertiary impacts on all groups rather than immediate optics.

cards.front: The Broken Window Fallacy: Visible Benefits Mask Invisible Costs
cards.back: Believing destruction stimulates trade. It accounts for visible income to the glazier, but completely ignores what the baker would have bought if his window weren't broken.
cards.takeaway: Destruction never creates wealth; it merely diverts scarce capital from productive innovation into maintenance.

cards.front: Opportunity Cost: The True Price of Every Economic Choice
cards.back: The real cost of deploying time, labor, or capital into any initiative is the exact value of the next best alternative you had to abandon.
cards.takeaway: Saying 'yes' to a mediocre project is implicitly saying 'no' to your highest-leverage opportunity.

title: Nudge: Improving Decisions
author: Richard Thaler & Cass Sunstein
summary: How subtle shifts in choice architecture guide humans toward healthier, wealthier, and wiser decisions.

cards.front: The Power of Defaults: Designing Environments That Guide Action
cards.back: Status Quo Bias causes the vast majority of users to stick with pre-selected options, perceiving any switch as cognitive effort or risk.
cards.takeaway: By making the optimal choice the default (opt-out instead of opt-in), adoption rates often leap from 20% to over 85%.

cards.front: Libertarian Paternalism: Helping People Choose Better Without Mandates
cards.back: It influences choice architecture to steer behavior in beneficial directions while strictly preserving the freedom to opt out easily and cheaply.
cards.takeaway: Never restrict choices when you can instead redesign the environment to make good choices frictionless.

title: Antifragile: Things That Gain from Disorder
author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
summary: Some things benefit from shocks; they thrive and grow when exposed to volatility, randomness, and stress.

cards.front: Beyond Resilience: Systems That Grow Stronger Under Stress
cards.back: The resilient or robust resists shocks and stays the same; the antifragile gets better, stronger, and smarter after absorbing stress.
cards.takeaway: Over-protecting systems from minor volatility makes them fragile to catastrophic Black Swan crashes.

cards.front: The Barbell Strategy: Extreme Safety Paired with Asymmetric Upside
cards.back: Playing it safe in 90% of assets (hyper-conservative) while taking high-upside asymmetric bets with the remaining 10% (hyper-aggressive), avoiding the fragile middle.
cards.takeaway: Eliminate ruin risk completely while maintaining boundless positive convexity.

title: The Psychology of Money
author: Morgan Housel
summary: Doing well with money has a little to do with how smart you are and a lot to do with how you behave.

cards.front: The Compounding Flywheel: Time in the Market Beats Raw Timing
cards.back: Buffett began investing at age 10. Time in the market exponentializes linear gains into astronomical compounding.
cards.takeaway: The secret to compounding isn't chasing maximum returns; it's surviving downturns consistently without interrupting the curve.

cards.front: Being Rich vs. Being Wealthy: Visible Spending vs. Hidden Freedom
cards.back: Rich is current income and visible spending (cars, jewelry, status symbols). Wealth is options, unspent capital, and freedom over your daily time.
cards.takeaway: Spending money to show people how much money you have is the fastest way to have less money.

title: Principles: Life and Work
author: Ray Dalio
summary: Systematic rules for decision-making developed at Bridgewater Associates.

cards.front: The 5-Step Machine: Goals, Problems, Diagnosis, Design, Execution
cards.back: 1. Set clear goals. 2. Identify problems and don't tolerate them. 3. Diagnose root causes. 4. Design plans. 5. Push through to execution.
cards.takeaway: Most people fail at step 2 and 3 because confronting personal weaknesses triggers painful ego defense mechanisms.

cards.front: Idea Meritocracy: Radically Transparent & Believability-Weighted Choices
cards.back: An organization where the best ideas win regardless of title, determined through radical transparency and believability-weighted decision making.
cards.takeaway: Weight opinions by a person's demonstrated track record and logical coherence, not rank or charisma.

title: The Intelligent Investor
author: Benjamin Graham
summary: The definitive book on value investing and building a margin of safety against market manic depression.

cards.front: The Parable of Mr. Market: Profit from Emotion Rather Than Joining It
cards.back: Mr. Market is your business partner who shows up every day offering to buy or sell shares at wild price swings. You are free to ignore him or exploit his mood swings.
cards.takeaway: The market is there to serve you, not to instruct you. Price is what you pay; value is what you get.

cards.front: Margin of Safety: Protecting Capital Against Unpredictable Futures
cards.back: Purchasing assets at a significant discount to their conservatively appraised intrinsic value to protect against errors in estimation and adverse luck.
cards.takeaway: The secret to sound investment can be condensed into three words: Margin of Safety.

title: Good Strategy / Bad Strategy
author: Richard Rumelt
summary: Cutting through empty corporate buzzwords to uncover the essential kernel of true strategic power.

cards.front: The Kernel of Strategy: Clear Diagnosis, Guiding Policy, Coherent Actions
cards.back: 1. A Diagnosis (simplifying the challenge). 2. A Guiding Policy (the overarching approach). 3. Coherent Actions (coordinated resource commitments).
cards.takeaway: A strategy that lacks actionable trade-offs and sacrifice is merely an empty wish list.

cards.front: Deconstructing Bad Strategy: Mistaking Wishful Thinking for Real Focus
cards.back: Look for four hallmarks: Fluff (fancy jargon hiding absence of thought), Failure to face challenge, Mistaking goals for strategy, and Bad strategic objectives.
cards.takeaway: If a plan claims to pursue 15 simultaneous priorities without trade-offs, it has zero strategy.

title: Zero to One
author: Peter Thiel
summary: Notes on startups and how to build breakthrough technology that creates new categories.

cards.front: The Contrarian Secret: Building What Truly Matters That Others Miss
cards.back: 'What important truth do very few people agree with you on?'
cards.takeaway: Brilliant business ideas usually look like bad or trivial ideas to consensus thinkers, shielding them from early competition.

cards.front: Monopoly Over Competition: Creating Uncontested Value from 0 to 1
cards.back: Perfect competition destroys margins and turns products into undifferentiated commodities. Enduring value is captured only by creative monopolies.
cards.takeaway: Aim to dominate a small, specific niche market first before scaling into adjacent markets.

title: The Innovator's Dilemma
author: Clayton M. Christensen
summary: Why great firms can fail because they do everything right for existing customers while missing disruptive shifts.

cards.front: Disruptive Innovation: Why Market Leaders Fail by Doing Everything Right
cards.back: Sustaining tech improves product performance for mainstream customers. Disruptive tech starts inferior and cheaper at the low end or in new markets, but steadily improves until it overtakes incumbents.
cards.takeaway: Incumbents rarely lose because of incompetence; they lose because listening to their best customers makes low-margin disruption look irrational.

title: Clean Code
author: Robert C. Martin
summary: A handbook of agile software craftsmanship and best practices for writing maintainable software.

cards.front: The Boy Scout Rule: Always Leave Code Cleaner Than You Found It
cards.back: 'Always leave the campground cleaner than you found it.' Whenever you touch code, make it slightly cleaner than when you opened it.
cards.takeaway: Continuous micro-refactoring prevents technical debt from accumulating into unmanageable architecture rot.

cards.front: Single Responsibility Principle: Code Should Do One Thing and Do It Well
cards.back: A module or function should have one, and only one, reason to change.
cards.takeaway: Functions should do one thing, do it well, and do it only.

title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications
author: Martin Kleppmann
summary: The fundamental principles, trade-offs, and architectures behind reliable distributed storage and computation systems.

cards.front: Reliability, Scalability, and Maintainability: The Architectural Trinity
cards.back: 1. Reliability (continues to work correctly under faults). 2. Scalability (handles traffic/data growth gracefully). 3. Maintainability (easy to evolve).
cards.takeaway: Failures are inevitable in distributed systems; resilience comes from tolerating faults, not pretending they won't occur.

cards.front: The CAP Theorem: Partition Tolerance and the Trade-Off of Consistency
cards.back: In a network partition (P), you must choose between Consistency (all nodes see latest data) or Availability (every request gets a response).
cards.takeaway: Network partitions are unavoidable; your architecture must decide whether to fail loud or return potentially stale data.

title: Meditations
author: Marcus Aurelius
summary: Private journal entries of the Roman Emperor on self-discipline, mortality, and emotional clarity.

cards.front: The Dichotomy of Control: Mastery Over Perception, Surrender to the Rest
cards.back: Some things are within our power (beliefs, desires, aversions, actions) and other things are not (reputation, wealth, other people's behavior, fate).
cards.takeaway: Suffering occurs when we tie our peace of mind to external variables we cannot guarantee.

cards.front: The Obstacle Is the Way: Transforming Adversity into Fuel for Character
cards.back: 'The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.'
cards.takeaway: Every crisis or unfair obstacle is raw material to practice patience, creativity, and virtue.
